question: On 17 August 2026, the Czech Government approved the repeal of the existing Strategy for Providing Information on European Affairs and the drafting of a new strategy. This is also set to include the closure of the network of regional Eurocentres in its current form.

For more than 20 years, Eurocentres have been maintaining contact with the public in the regions, cooperating with schools, libraries, universities and governments, and organising around 1 300 events per year. The Government is justifying the change on the grounds of modernising communication and making greater use of digital tools.

However, it is not yet clear how their regional and educational activities will be replaced, even though steps have already been taken to end the current network. Furthermore, in Liberec, Karlovy Vary and Jihlava, the Eurocentres are directly linked to EUROPE DIRECT centres, whose activities for the period between 2026 and 2030 are largely funded by the Commission. 1.

Is the Commission monitoring the situation with regard to the Czech Government’s decision to close the Eurocentre network and its possible effects on the availability of information on the EU for Czech citizens, especially in the regions, and how does it assess this decision?

Was the Commission or its Representation in the Czech Republic consulted by the Czech Government before this decision was adopted, and did the Czech Government inform the Commission of the specific system it intends to use to replace the Eurocentres’ existing regional information and education activities?

What repercussions might the closure of the Eurocentres have for the operations and funding of the EUROPE DIRECT centres in Liberec, Karlovy Vary and Jihlava, and how does the Commission intend to ensure the continuity of their activities during the 2026‑2030 financial period?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.11.2026) The Commission engages with citizens through a wide range of communication channels, including EUROPE DIRECT Centres. They share useful information about EU initiatives and citizens’ rights, organise local events and open discussions1.

In the Czech Republic, there are currently 12 centres operating, three of which are hosted by Euro Info Centres run by the Czech government. The cooperation between these centres and the Commission is governed by a partnership agreement.

In this context, the Commission received formal notice regarding the termination of the partnership and is taking the necessary steps to ensure the continuity of communication activities in the respective regions, including, where appropriate, the possible selection of other centres via a public call. The Commission is closely monitoring the situation and maintains an ongoing dialogue with the competent authorities.

The Treaties lay down principles2 that underpin the right of citizens to be well informed, so that they can participate in the democratic life of the EU. The Commission’s EU Strategy for Civil Society3 reflects its efforts to work closely with Member States to promote and sustain dialogue with civil society and citizens.
The way in which Member States communicate European affairs within their respective structures falls within their competence.

1 https://european-union.europa.eu/contact-eu/meet-us/find-closest-europe-direct-centre_en. 2 Articles 2 and 10 of the Treaty on the European Union (TEU), Article 11 of the TEU, Article 15 of the Treaty
on the Functioning of the European Union, Article 1(2) and Article 4(3) of the TEU. 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=comnat:COM_2025_0790_FIN.
